---
title: "Estimating EIR from prevalence"
---

```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.style.use("styles/mint.mplstyle")
```

A parasite survey gives prevalence. The transmission model requires an EIR, so `estimint`
inverts the one into the other, returning the EIR that would have produced the prevalence you
measured. The inversion does not run on prevalence alone. The model takes six covariates
describing the setting alongside it.

## The prevalence model

Load it by name. The model is bundled in the wheel, so the call is offline and takes
milliseconds.

```{python}
import pandas as pd
from estimint import load_xgb_model, run_xgb_model

prev_model = load_xgb_model("prevalence")
prev_model["features"]
```

All seven columns are required. Six of them describe the setting, and the seventh, `prev_y9`,
carries the driving input.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dn0_use` | Probability a mosquito dies on contact with a net. From `calculate_dn0`. |
| `Q0` | Human blood index, 0 to 1 |
| `phi_bednets` | Share of bites taken while people are in bed |
| `seasonal` | 0 perennial, 1 strongly seasonal |
| `itn_use` | ITN coverage, 0 to 1. From `calculate_dn0`. |
| `irs_use` | IRS coverage, 0 to 1 |
| `prev_y9` | Parasite prevalence in the deployment year, 0 to 1 |

A missing column raises a `ValueError` naming it. `prevalence` is accepted as an alias for
`prev_y9` and copied across for you, which is convenient, because it is also the column name
`estimate_eir_with_mosquito_delta` expects.

`run_xgb_model` takes the frame and the model, and returns a plain NumPy array. One element
per row.

```{python}
setting = dict(
    dn0_use=0.33, Q0=0.87, phi_bednets=0.82,
    seasonal=0.0, itn_use=0.6, irs_use=0.0,
)

one = pd.DataFrame([{**setting, "prevalence": 0.30}])
eir = run_xgb_model(one, prev_model)

type(eir), eir
```

A prevalence of 30% in this setting implies about 13.4 infectious bites per person per
year.

## The shape of the relationship

Holding the setting fixed and sweeping the prevalence shows how the EIR behaves.

```{python}
sweep = pd.DataFrame(
    [{**setting, "prevalence": p} for p in [0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.45, 0.60, 0.75]]
)
sweep["eir"] = run_xgb_model(sweep, prev_model)

sweep[["prevalence", "eir"]].round(2)
```

The EIR is nowhere near linear in prevalence. Doubling prevalence from 0.30 to 0.60 does not
double the EIR but raises it roughly fivefold. Between 0.60 and 0.75 the EIR more than doubles
again.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Inferred EIR against prevalence, holding the setting fixed."
#| fig-alt: "A line rising slowly from near zero at 5% prevalence then climbing very steeply above 60% prevalence, reaching about 160 infectious bites per person per year at 75%."
import numpy as np

grid = pd.DataFrame([{**setting, "prevalence": p} for p in np.linspace(0.05, 0.75, 71)])
grid["eir"] = run_xgb_model(grid, prev_model)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(grid["prevalence"], grid["eir"], color="#00d4aa")
ax.set_xlabel("Prevalence")
ax.set_ylabel("EIR (infectious bites per person per year)")
plt.show()
```

Precision in the prevalence you supply therefore matters far more at the top of the range than
at the bottom. An input that is a few points out at 70% prevalence moves the inferred EIR by
tens of bites per year.

## The role of the setting

If EIR were a function of prevalence alone, a lookup table would do the job and no model
would be needed.

The district in the running example has a measured prevalence of 0.45, pyrethroid
resistance of 0.30, and pyrethroid-only nets. In the sweep below the net coverage is the
only quantity that varies, and the measured prevalence is held at 0.45 throughout.

```{python}
from estimint import calculate_dn0

rows = []
for coverage in [0.0, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9]:
    nets = calculate_dn0(0.30, py_only=coverage)
    rows.append({
        "coverage": coverage,
        "dn0_use": nets.dn0,
        "itn_use": nets.itn_use,
        "Q0": 0.85, "phi_bednets": 0.80, "seasonal": 0.0, "irs_use": 0.0,
        "prevalence": 0.45,
    })

nets_vs_eir = pd.DataFrame(rows)
nets_vs_eir["eir"] = run_xgb_model(nets_vs_eir, prev_model)

nets_vs_eir[["coverage", "dn0_use", "itn_use", "prevalence", "eir"]].round(3)
```

Every row reports the same prevalence. The inferred EIR rises by roughly two thirds across the
column. That is why understating `itn_use`, the error described in
[Nets and dn0](nets-and-dn0.qmd), biases the inferred EIR downwards. It is also why the same
measured prevalence in two districts with different net coverage does not imply the same
transmission.

## The global model

Passing the model to every call is repetitive. `set_global_model` registers one as the default,
after which `run_xgb_model` may be called with the frame alone.

```{python}
from estimint import set_global_model, get_global_model

set_global_model(prev_model)
run_xgb_model(one)
```

`get_global_model` returns whatever is registered, or `None` if nothing is.

```{python}
get_global_model()["class"]
```

That is a convenience for interactive work. In a script that touches more than one of the three
models, pass the model explicitly. The global slot holds exactly one, and a stray
`set_global_model` elsewhere in the session will change what an unqualified call resolves to.

::: {.callout-note}
## The valid range

`prev_y9` is clamped to `[0.005, 0.80]`. Values outside that band are quietly pulled to the
nearest edge, and no warning is raised.

```{python}
edges = pd.DataFrame(
    [{**setting, "prevalence": p} for p in [0.001, 0.005, 0.80, 0.95]]
)
edges["eir"] = run_xgb_model(edges, prev_model)

edges[["prevalence", "eir"]].round(3)
```

A prevalence of 0.001 and one of 0.005 return the same EIR, as do 0.80 and 0.95. The
model reports nothing unusual. If a sweep of prevalences produces an implausibly flat EIR
at either end, the cause is almost always this clamp rather than the epidemiology.
:::
